cues.text: Hey, welcome back.
A lens changes a ray's direction at two refracting surfaces.
In the thin lens approximation, we represent those two changes at one plane
through the optical center.
A converging lens brings parallel paraxial rays to a focus on the far side.
A diverging lens makes them spread, as though they came from a focus on the
incoming side.
We'll keep incident light traveling left to right and rightward distances
positive.
For a real object to the left, u is negative.
A converging lens has positive f, and a diverging lens has negative f in the
medium being considered.
The thin lens equation is one over f equals one over v minus one over u.
Notice the minus between the image and object terms.
Do not carry over the mirror equation.
Lens magnification is v over u, without the mirror's extra minus sign.
To draw a converging lens image, send one ray parallel to the axis: it
refracts
through the far focus.
A ray through the optical center is undeviated in this ideal thin lens
treatment.
Their intersection locates the image tip.
Our drawings are paraxial schematics, not exact wide angle lens designs.
The point is to connect the image geometry to the signed distances rather than
memorize disconnected cases.
Let's put a real object thirty centimeters before a converging lens of focal
length ten centimeters.
Before calculating, locate it: thirty is greater than twice ten.
We expect a real, inverted, smaller image on the other side.
Now use signs.
f is positive ten, and u is negative thirty.
One over v equals one over f plus one over u.
That is one tenth minus one thirtieth, or one fifteenth per centimeter.
Therefore v is positive fifteen centimeters.
The image lies between the far focus and twice the focal length.
Magnification is fifteen divided by negative thirty, or negative one half.
A four centimeter high upright object gives a signed image height negative two
centimeters.
The image is two centimeters tall and inverted.
A screen placed at that image plane can intercept the converging light.
This is what real means; it is not a statement that virtual images cannot be
seen.
Try moving the object to twenty centimeters.
Take a moment.
u equals negative twenty, so v is positive twenty, and magnification is
negative one.
The image is real, inverted, and the same size.
The ray sketch and the arithmetic tell the same story.
For a JEE answer, report location, orientation, and size together, and keep
every length in the same unit before combining reciprocals.
Move our object inside the converging lens's focal distance.
With f positive ten centimeters and u negative five, one over v is one tenth
minus one fifth, or negative one tenth.
The image distance is negative ten centimeters, on the object side.
Magnification is negative ten divided by negative five, so positive two.
Refraction sends the rays apart, but their backward extensions meet at an
upright, enlarged virtual image.
This is how a simple magnifying lens can help us inspect a small object.
A virtual image is not captured directly on a screen at its apparent location.
Your eye can still form its own real image from the arriving rays.
Now switch to a diverging lens with f negative ten centimeters and a real
object at negative thirty.
One over v is negative one tenth minus one thirtieth, giving v negative seven
point five centimeters.
Magnification is positive one quarter.
The image is virtual, upright, and smaller, between the lens and its incoming
side focus.
For a real object, that diminished virtual pattern is dependable for a
diverging lens.
Virtual objects created by another element need separate analysis.
Finally, if a real object sits exactly at a converging focus, the outgoing
paraxial rays are parallel.
Image distance is at infinity, not an ordinary finite number.
Predict the case first, then use the equation as a check.
Where does a lens's focal length come from?
Combining the refraction equations for its two surfaces gives the lens maker
relation.
For a thin lens surrounded by the same medium on both sides, one over f equals
the lens index relative to that medium, minus one, times one over R one minus
one over R two.
The radii are signed using our left to right convention.
A symmetric biconvex glass lens in air, with index one point five, has first
radius positive twenty centimeters and second radius negative twenty.
Subtracting their reciprocals gives one tenth per centimeter.
Multiplying by zero point five gives one twentieth, so f is positive twenty
centimeters.
Now imagine immersing it in a surrounding medium with exactly the same
refractive index as the lens.
The relative index factor becomes zero.
There is no refraction at the ideal matched boundaries, the power vanishes,
and
the focal length is infinite.
If the surrounding index exceeds the lens index, even this biconvex shape can
become diverging.
That is why shape labels alone are not enough without the medium.
The formula assumes negligible thickness, small ray angles, and a common
surrounding index.
A thick lens or different media on the two sides needs more careful treatment.
In JEE calculations, draw the centers of curvature to assign radius signs
instead of calling every radius positive.
Optical power measures how strongly a lens converges or diverges paraxial
light.
It is one over focal length when the focal length is expressed in meters.
Its unit is the diopter, equivalent to inverse meters.
A positive twenty centimeter lens has focal length zero point two meters and
power positive five diopters.
A negative fifty centimeter lens has power negative two diopters.
Put these ideal thin lenses in contact, in the same surrounding medium.
Their powers add, giving positive three diopters.
The effective focal length is one third of a meter, about thirty three point
three centimeters.
Positive total power tells us the pair is converging.
Why does addition work?
When the planes coincide in the thin lens model, the second lens adds its ray
deflection contribution to the first at essentially the same ray height.
If the lenses are separated, that height changes during the travel between
them.
The simple contact rule is then insufficient.
Also, do not add focal lengths.
Five diopters plus negative two diopters is meaningful; twenty centimeters
plus
negative fifty centimeters does not give the combined focal length.
Our final routine is to choose the right relation, assign signs, convert units
where required, and interpret the resulting image or power.
The next classes will apply those same habits to prisms and optical
instruments.
